claims.text: A localized thermal or laser surface treatment can induce nanoscale coherent precipitates in an HEA.
The induced precipitates will be concentrated in the surface and near-surface regions.
The induced precipitates can be enriched in a soft, lubricious element such as Ag.
The treatment will remain tribologically effective from room temperature to approximately 800 °C.
The coherent nanoprecipitates will form a distributed network at the surface and in near-surface layers.
The proposed nanoprecipitates have low shear strength.
Coherent precipitate interfaces relieve local stress concentrations.
The nanoprecipitates reduce shear stress at the tribological contact interface.
The nanoprecipitates create a self-healing boundary-lubricant layer.
The boundary layer minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation motion or transmission.
Facilitated dislocation motion promotes easier sliding at the contact interface.
The treated HEA will have a lower coefficient of friction than the untreated HEA.
The treated HEA will have a lower wear rate than the untreated HEA.
The friction and wear improvements will persist across a wide temperature range.
The relative reductions in friction and wear may be on the order of tens of percent.
A uniform and coherent nanoprecipitate distribution is required for the beneficial tribological effects.
An inhomogeneous or thermally or cyclically unstable precipitate network will diminish the treatment's effectiveness.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that benefits are conditional on successfully obtaining a uniform coherent precipitate network, whereas the falsification rule treats failure of the treatment to produce that network as falsification of the causal hypothesis. Failure to realize the stipulated mediator is a manipulation failure rather than a decisive test of whether that mediator would reduce friction and wear.
